title: Low-strength geopolymer concrete by complete replacement of sodium silicate using sugarcane bagasse ash and sodium hydroxide
abstract: Abstract Conventional geopolymer concrete (CGPC) includes sodium silicate (Na 2 SiO 3 ), whose production is associated with relatively high energy consumption and CO 2  emissions. This study investigates the potential use of sugarcane bagasse ash (SCBA) as a sustainable replacement for sodium silicate. Sugarcane bagasse (SCB), an important Queensland agricultural by product, is often under-utilised, with factory-burnt SCB typically dumped or used as low-quality fertiliser. In this research, factory-burnt SCB, was processed into SCBA, and employed to create an alkaline activator (AA). Suitable furnace-treatment conditions were first determined to valorise the factory-burnt SCB through characterisation studies such as Scanning electron microscopy, X-ray fluorescence, X-ray diffraction and Thermogravimetric analysis. Results show a notable increase in overall silica content of SCBA from 78 to 84% and enhanced thermal stability. Three trials were conducted to explore the viability of SCBA-based AA in greener concrete: Trial 1 and 2 were carried out to investigate the incorporation of SCBA-based AA in, respectively, Ground Granulated Blast-furnace Slag (GGBS)-based and Fly Ash (FA)-based GPC. On completion of the two trials, Trial 3 was conducted to explore the potential for strength improvement using a superplasticiser to reduce water content. SCBA-based GPC achieved compressive strengths between 3 and 5 MPa, indicating its potential for low-strength concrete applications. Moreover, the cradle-to-gate approach indicated a 10% to 30% reduction in carbon footprint, depending on transport considerations. The resulting SGPC shows potential for non-structural applications such as masonry units with significantly lowered embodied carbon compared to CGPC.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Alkaline-activated binders (AAB) are becoming popular nowadays as sustainable alternatives to ordinary Portland cement (OPC), due to their improved mechanical, durability characteristics and notably reduced emissions of CO 2  [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. AABs are prepared through the geopolymerization process of aluminosilicate precursors such as fly ash (FA), ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS), and metakaolin, and different types of alkaline activators.

Among these activators, sodium silicate is widely used for its high silica content, but its production requires a temperature range of 1200 °C–1400 °C [ 4 ], making it both costly [ 5 ] and environmentally polluting [ 6 ,  7 ]. Turner and Collins (2013) [ 8 ] explained that the CO 2  footprint of GPC was observed to be only 9% lower than OPCC, with a major segment due to the sodium silicate. This data evidence the importance of replacing sodium silicate to improve the CO 2  footprint reduction percentage. Consistently, the handbook on alkali-activated cement-based binders (AACB) suggests that there exists a notable gap concerning environmentally beneficial and economically viable activators [ 9 ].

A few studies suggested the feasibility of sugarcane bagasse ash (SCBA)-NaOH activator as an alternative for the commercial AA system [ 7 ,  10 ], but despite very high strength gains, the treatment processes were associated with high energy consumption. The related literature reports that controlled furnace treatment of SCBA at 700 °C to enhance pozzolanic activity [ 11 ], furnace treatment with oxygen feeding after acid washing to achieve 91.57 wt% silica [ 12 ], and combined high-temperature, acid, and alkaline treatments yielding up to 88.13 wt% silica [ 13 ]. A study investigating the replacement of commercial sodium silicate with SCBA treated with NaOH at higher temperatures found that the resulting compressive strength was only 1.87% lower than the specimens prepared with commercial solutions [ 14 ]. Other approaches involve furnace treatment of SCBA and mixing with NaOH at high temperature to produce geopolymer strengths of 16–32.9 MPa [ 7 ,  10 ].

While these studies suggest the potential of SCBA to be treated through high-energy intensive processes to achieve qualities for high-strength concrete production under controlled curing, the feasibility of using less-intensive treatment options under ambient curing has not been yet explored. Given the above-mentioned energy-intensive and controlled-curing processes, it was considered that further studies on valorisation of factory-burned SCBA, especially after only brief pretreatment processes and under ambient curing conditions merits further investigation.

To this end, Queensland factory-burned SCBA [ 15 ] was obtained and, after a brief pre-treatment process, was subjected to a microstructural characterisation study, to understand about the effect of treatment processes qualitatively and quantitatively. Scanning Electron Microscopy, X-Ray Diffraction, X-Ray Fluorescence, and Thermogravimetric analysis were conducted. The purpose of the SEM analysis was to qualitatively examine the morphological changes in SCBA resulting from thermal treatment although particle size ranges were also determined both before and after treatments. The material was then used through several trials to create concrete mixtures. The study concludes with a critical evaluation of the concrete mixtures from density, strength, and carbon footprint perspectives.

sections.heading: Raw materials
paragraphs: The dry raw materials used in the study are depicted in Fig.  1 . Fly ash and GGBS were used as precursors, and SCBA was used as an alternative to sodium silicate in AA. River sand (specific gravity − 2.71 g/cm 3 , moisture content − 0.23) and 20 mm crushed stone (specific gravity − 3.01 g/cm 3 , moisture content − 1.32) purchased from a local supplier, were utilised as fine and coarse aggregates, respectively. Class F fly ash, GGBS, and factory-burnt SCB were sourced, respectively, from Millmerran Fly Ash, Wagners, and Mackay Sugar, all in Queensland. The factory-burnt SCBA was a byproduct of energy production using a 200 t/hr boiler. In addition, for conventional GPC, commercially available sodium hydroxide pellets and sodium silicate solution were utilised, with the properties summarised in Table  1 . The specific gravities of the FA and GGBS were determined by using an Anton-Paar pycnometer and found to be 2.04 g/cm 3  and 2.60 g/cm 3 , respectively. The moisture contents of fly ash and GGBS were determined to be 0.07% and 0.30%, respectively, according to ASTMC599-19 [ 16 ]. The particle size distribution of precursors and the particle size distribution of aggregates are provided Fig.  2 . The poorly graded particle distribution of aggregates may attribute to the higher void spaces within the GPC mixture. when incorporating in GPC. The key volumetric percentiles such as Dx(10), Dx(50) and Dx(90) obtained from the analysis are 3.22, 14.6, and 44.9 for fly ash, and 3.19, 14.4, 45.1 for GGBS respectively. Fig. 2 Distribution curves of materials used in the study

sections.heading: SCBA treatment and AA preparation
paragraphs: For conventional AA, the required amount of NaOH pellets was weighed in a small beaker. About 75% of the required water was placed in a volumetric flask, which was set in an ice/water bath and kept inside the fume hood on the magnetic stirrer at 400 rpm. NaOH pellets were then added slowly to ensure a controlled exothermic reaction. Finally, the remaining water was transferred to the volumetric flask. During the concrete mixing, both sodium hydroxide solution and sodium silicate are added to the GPC as commercial AA (Fig.  4 a).

A thermochemical treatment process was employed to activate the SCBA for SCBA-based AA. For Trial 1, this process included subjecting factory-burnt SCB to 700 °C temperatures for 90 min in a K2FL muffle furnace. It was decided in subsequent trials to find an efficient treatment temperature considering characterisation test results and energy consumption considerations. For this purpose, a furnace was separately programmed to ramp up to three different temperatures (500 °C, 600 °C, and 700 °C), each time at a heating rate of 800 °C/hour. Upon reaching the target temperature, the samples were treated for three different time durations (30, 60, and 90 min), resulting in a total of 9 treatment scenarios. Then, SCBA was sieved using 0.6 mm as per the study of Mansaneira et al. (2017) [ 17 ]. SCBA treated at 500 °C for 30 min was selected for the replacement. The particle size distribution of SCBA treated at 700 °C for 90 min and 500 °C for 30 min is provided in Fig.  2 a. The key volumetric percentiles such as Dx(10), Dx(50) and Dx(90) obtained from the analysis are 18.9, 72, and 197 for SCBA treated at 700 °C for 90 min, and 16.7, 72.3, 224 for SCBA treated at 500 °C for 30 min respectively. Notable, both the SCBAs appeared in approximately similar distribution despite their treatment conditions, may be due to the sieving process. The treatment programme of factory burnt SCB is detailed in Fig.  3 . Fig. 3 Furnace treatment process of factory-burnt SCB

Weighed portions of SCBA were then gradually added to NaOH solution using a small beaker under constant stirring. This solution was then stirred vigorously for one hour to facilitate the dissolution of silica from the SCBA. Physical comparison of conventional AA and SCBA-based AA is depicted in Fig.  4 . The resulting AA solution was transferred to a plastic container and gently agitated periodically to prevent premature polymerisation. After mixing, the solution was used to make the SCBA-based GPC mixture. Fig. 4 Comparative visuals of different AAs

sections.heading: Characterisation tests
paragraphs: To investigate material morphology, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) analysis was conducted using a Phenom XLG2 machine. An accelerating voltage of 5 kV was selected to optimise image resolution and facilitate surface feature identification. The beam intensity was set to ‘image’ mode, and a secondary electron detector (SED) was utilised to capture the morphological characteristics of the samples. A thin layer of gold (‘Au’) was coated onto the samples to enhance their electrical conductivity. An “EVACTRON” plasma cleaner was employed for 5 min to remove hydrocarbon residues from the sample surface.

The SCBA samples exhibited a heterogeneous particle morphology (Fig.  5 ). Analysis revealed the presence of various particle shapes, including spherical (I), prismatic (II), fibrous (III), and irregular (IV) shapes. It is noteworthy that past studies report that spherical particles, often formed through high-temperature melting processes, were found to contain Si, and O, as well as minor amounts of Na, K, Al, Mg, and Ca, whereas prismatic particles primarily consisted of Si and O [ 18 ,  19 ]. Irregular-shaped particles were identified as the major source of amorphous content within the ash [ 20 ]. Furnace treatment resulted in a notable shift in particle morphology. An apparent reduction in the particle size was observed from [1–200 µm] for SCB to [1–150 µm] for SCBA in the tested specimen, suggesting the alteration of morphology by furnace treatment process. In addition, an apparent increase in the proportion of prismatic particles was also observed. While SEM provided limited quantitative evidence, these observations corroborate the findings of XRF and XRD results, which indicates an increased silica content due to the furnace treatment. Also, the presence of irregular porous particles may contribute to the increment of water demand. Concurrently, a decrease in the number of fibrous particles was observed, likely attributed to their complete combustion during the treatment process. However, treatment at 700 °C, a relatively higher temperature, may promote the formation of non-reactive crystalline silica. Fly ash particles exhibited a spherical morphology with rounded angularity and a mostly smooth surface Fig.  5 d. Hollow (V) and encapsulating smaller spheres (VI) [ 21 ] are visible in the output. Conversely, GGBS particles displayed a flaky and elongated morphology with sharp, angular edges and a rough surface texture Fig.  5 e. Both the precursors exhibited the particle dimension ranging from 1 to 50 µm. Fig. 5 SEM images of raw and refined materials

Quantitative chemical characterisation of the samples was performed using X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy, which analyses the characteristic X-ray emissions produced by elements. A Bruker S8 Tiger Series II Wavelength Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence (WD-XRF) Spectrometer was employed for this analysis. A Katanax X-600 automatic fusion machine was used to prepare fused glass discs for XRF analysis.

The XRF analysis revealed that the dominant constituents present in fly ash are silica (SiO 2 ) (57.4%), and alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) (34.2%), while GGBS has SiO 2  (34.2%), Al 2 O 3  (15.1%), and calcium oxide (CaO) (42.3%) as the major components (Table  2 ). This chemical composition demonstrates the suitability of fly ash and GGBS as aluminosilicate precursors in the production of geopolymer concrete. The high content of silica and alumina in both materials provides the necessary framework for the formation of the geopolymer gel, the key component responsible for the strength and durability of geopolymer concrete.

Al 2 O 3  and SiO 2  are the predominant constituents within both factory-burnt SCB and SCBA. This observation, particularly the high percentage of silica and alumina in the SCBA, aligns with findings from previous studies by [ 22 ,  23 – 24 ], which have demonstrated the potential of SCBA to function as a precursor material in GPC production. Notably, the factory-burnt SCB exhibited a remarkably high silica content (SiO 2 ) of 77.8%, a characteristic highly beneficial for GPC production, particularly when aiming to replace sodium silicate in the activator solution. The furnace treatment process significantly enhanced the overall chemical composition of the factory-burnt SCB. This treatment resulted in an increase in the content of all constituent oxides, most notably silica, which increased from nearly 78% to approximately 84%, while simultaneously reducing the loss of ignition mass. It was found that for the same temperature, the overall silica content generally increased with treatment duration. Conversely, for the same treatment durations, a consistent trend could not be identified for the increase in silica content vs increase in the temperature as previously suggested by Embong et al. (2016) [ 25 ]. For example, in the 90-min duration, the 500 °C temperature produced the highest amount of silica of all (500 °C, 600°, and 700°) scenarios. Likewise, for the same 30-min duration from 500 °C to 600 °C, the results did not support the previous findings. This discrepancy is attributed to the inherent heterogeneity of factory-burnt SCB sample, specifically the potentially irregular distribution of unburnt bagasse and soil contaminants throughout the subsamples. It is also highlighted that the difference between the highest and the lowest silica content observed across all treatment conditions was relatively small (2.33 wt%).

An X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was undertaken to compare the relative intensity of peaks due to crystalline components for the raw and treated materials. A Bruker D8 Advance powder diffractometer operating in Bragg–Brentano geometry with a cobalt source (35 kV, 40 mA) was employed to identify the components of raw and refined sugarcane bagasse ash. Patterns were collected for 60 min from 2° to 90°2 θ  at a step size of 0.015°. The XRD patterns of the materials used in the study are provided in Fig.  6 . Phase identification was performed using the PDF5 + database (ICDD, 2024) in EVA (V7, Bruker). The Rietveld method implemented in TOPAS (V7, Bruker) was used for refinement and quantitative phase analysis. Peak shapes were modelled via an instrument function determined from the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) Standard Reference Material (SRM) 660a (LaB 6 ). Fig. 6 XRD patterns of raw and refined materials

The XRD analysis revealed the prominent crystalline phases identified in fly ash included Mullite and Quartz with an amorphous content of 67.8%. For GGBS, the major crystalline phases were Calcite and Gypsum, with an amorphous content of 97.4% (Table  3 ). Comparatively higher presence of amorphous percentage of GGBS explains the early strength gaining quality of GGBS-based GPC than fly ash-based GPC.

The analysis also identified the presence of both crystalline and amorphous phases in both factory-burnt SCB and SCBA. Quartz was identified as the dominant crystalline phase in both materials. The presence of sand in the factory-burnt SCB likely contributed to the observed quartz content [ 26 ]. The factory-burnt SCB exhibited an initial amorphous content of 39.9%, which decreased to 33.6% and then raised to 33.8% following the furnace treatment at 700 °C for 90 min and then at 500 °C for 30 min. This reduction in amorphous silica content presents a potential challenge, as amorphous silica is crucial for the polymerisation reactions within the modified AA. While the increase in crystalline silica content, primarily in the form of quartz, is observed, it is important to note that crystalline silica, such as quartz, does not actively participate in the reaction with sodium hydroxide. The modified AA requires a significant amount of amorphous silica for effective polymerisation. Therefore, this study highlights the critical need to optimise the furnace treatment conditions by including various treatment temperatures and durations, considering the balance between amorphous silica content and energy consumption.

Thermogravimetry analysis (TGA) and derivative of thermogravimetry analysis (DTG) were performed to monitor the mass of the SCBA samples as a function of temperature in an N 2  atmosphere. TG and DTG were done on NETZSCH STA 449 F3 Jupiter, which can be heated up to 1500 °C. A Platina crucible with lids was selected to perform TGA tests, as platina does not react with SiO 2 , Al 2 O 3 , and MgO, which are present in the samples.

TG graph gives information on mass change with respect to temperature under thermogravimetric analysis, while DTG gives information on the rate of mass change with respect to temperature (Fig.  7 ). The x-axis shows the temperature (°C), and the y-axis shows the corresponding mass percentage (%) on the left side, and the rate of mass change on the right side (%/°C). Fly ash and GGBS exhibited better stability at elevated temperatures, with mass losses of 0.03% and 2.07%, respectively. The factory-burnt SCB exhibited a residual mass of 92.70% with comparatively higher mass loss, while the SCBA treated at 700 °C for 90 min showed a higher stability than the SCBA treated at 500 °C for 30 min. This observation can be attributed to the pre-treatment process, which likely enhances the thermal stability of the material. The initial mass loss observed in factory-burnt SCB can be attributed to the loss of moisture and the decomposition of volatile organic compounds. Subsequent mass loss is primarily associated with active pyrolysis [ 27 ]. A significant portion of this mass loss occurred prior to reaching 500 °C. The minimal mass loss at higher temperatures can be attributed to the combustion of residual hydrocarbons. The TGA results suggest the furnace treatment condition for SCBA at temperatures 500 °C or higher may contribute to better performance under extreme fire conditions, due to the observed reduction in mass loss percentages, compared to factory-burnt SCB. This is based on the powder materials not on hardened concrete. Fig. 7 TGA and DTG graphs

sections.heading: Concrete compression testing program
paragraphs: The test programme was designed to investigate the performance of the SCBA-based AA-incorporated GPCs regardless of the user’s chosen mixture design, which may have different activator compositions. The study evolved through several trials to evaluate the feasibility of sugarcane bagasse ash (SCBA) as an AA in SCBA-based AA incorporated GPC through three key trials. The consecutive trial mixtures were informed by the results from earlier phases.

sections.heading: Mixture design formation
paragraphs: Trial 1 was focused on examining a conventional GGBS-based GPC alongside three modified (SCBA-based) mixtures with varying SCBA/NaOH ratios. A conventional GGBS-based GPC was prepared using sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and sodium silicate (Na 2 SiO 3 ). Counterpart mixtures were then prepared using SCBA-based AA (NaOH and SCBA), as discussed previously.
While SCBA-based mixtures achieved 73% of the conventional concrete strength, it was decided to run a 2nd trial due to the compressive strength of the conventional GPC being only 6.4 MPa (at 7 days).

In Trial 2, an FA-based conventional mixture with high compressive strength in ambient curing conditions was targeted. In this Trial, the conventional FA-based GPC achieved 39.45 MPa in 28 days, but the SCBA-modified mixtures achieved only 3 MPa to 5 MPa. The reason for this large difference was attributed to the excessive water addition that was required to achieve the desired workability in SCBA-based mixtures. The addition resulted in the decrease of the effective molarity of NaOH and negatively impacted the geopolymerization reaction. This low strength prompted Trial 3, which entailed targeting the same FA-based GPC mixture as Trial 2 but with the addition of superplasticiser to reduce water in SCBA-based mixtures. As discussed later herein, the use of superplasticiser and the reduction in water usage did not significantly improve compressive strength.
In the following, the process of creating mixture designs is explained, with a detailed presentation of the test results.

In this report, Conventional GPC is denoted by CGPC-X, where X refers to the predominant precursor material (G for GGBS, F for fly ash). SCBA-based AA incorporated GPC is denoted by SGPCY-X, where X refers to the predominant precursor material, and Y indicates the SCBA/NaOH (s)  mass ratio. Finally, superplasticiser added SCBA-based AA incorporated GPC is denoted by SGPCSY-X, where the second S indicates superplasticiser (SP) addition, X refers to the predominant precursor material, and Y details the SCBA/NaOH mass ratio.

The mix proportions that were used in the three trials are detailed in Table  4 . In Trial 1, the GGBS-based conventional GPC (CGPC-G) mixture was developed following a procedure explained in [ 28 ]. The mass ratio (M +) of Na 2 O in the activation solution to dry binder mass was maintained at 7.5%, and the alkali modulus (AM) representing the Na 2 O/SiO 2  ratio in the alkaline solution was maintained at 1.25. The total solid mass of the binder, which included fly ash, GGBS, and solids from both sodium hydroxide and sodium silicate solutions, was used to calculate the required water content. It was assumed that both NaOH and Na 2 SiO 3  solutions contributed Na 2 O, while SiO 2  was provided exclusively by the Na 2 SiO 3  solution. This approach ensured precise control over the polymerisation components critical for geopolymer formation.

In this Trial, the mixture design for SCBA-based AA incorporated GPC (SGPC-G) was developed by formulating SCBA-derived AAs with identical mass ratios of sodium oxide to binder content (M +) and alkali moduli (AM) to maintain consistency in GPC production. M + and AM were calculated using Eq. ( 1 ) and Eq. ( 2 ). However, the incorporation of SCBA for modified AA production introduced uncertainties regarding its precise amorphous silica content. While XRD analysis served as a standard technique for phase identification, its limited sensitivity in quantifying amorphous phases [ 29 ] necessitated an experimental approach. The XRF results suggested that SCBA consisted of 83.13% of SiO 2 . Separately from XRD analysis, the SCBA has 33.8% of total amorphous content and 51.1% of Quartz, with a total sum of 84.9%. This value is 1.77% higher than the SiO 2  contents (83.13%) suggested from XRF results.

In Trial 1, GGBS-based mixture designs exhibited poor strength, low workability and visible surface cracking. In Trial 2, Fly ash-based conventional geopolymer (CGPC-F) was therefore adapted from [ 32 ] as an alternative, with a target compressive strength of 39.60 MPa and a slump of 110 mm. The M + value and AM value of the mixture were calculated as 12.6 and 1.05. The mixture design for the corresponding SCBA-based AA incorporated GPC (SGPC-F) was developed by calculating NaOH and SCBA contents by maintaining equal identity between M + and AM values of CGPC-F. Again, by using XRF and XRD results as a benchmark and assuming that not all the calculated amorphous silica content will react to produce sodium silicate, three modified mixtures, SGPC2.5-F, SGPC3.0-F, and SGPC3.5-F, were formulated with various amorphous silica contents (20%, 25%, and 30%) for SCBA.

In Trial 2, addition of SCBA to the mixture, increased the required water, which in turn negatively affected the compressive strength. Therefore, Sika viscocrete-1250 superplasticiser (density of 1.07 g/cm 3 ) was added at 1.2% of the binder content improve workability without the need for increased water. The study of Alaa M. Rashad (2017) [ 31 ] suggests that addition of silica fume could be explored for SCBA-based AA incorporated GPCs to improve workability and reducing water demand. When calculating the SCBA to NaOH mass ratio, a constant NaOH content was maintained in previous trials while SCBA proportions were varied as per the assumed amorphous silica content. But an opposite approach was adopted in Trial 3. For a constant SCBA content, NaOH content was adjusted to maintain the SCBA to NAOH mass ratio to be 1, 0.8 and 0.6 to test the effects of water addition. Three modified mixtures, SGPCS2.5-F, SGPCS2.0-F, and SGPCS1.5-F, were formulated. The M + values of the mixtures were calculated as 12.6, 15.76 and 21.03 respectively, and AM values were calculated as 1.05, 1.28 and 1.71 respectively.

sections.heading: Sample preparation
paragraphs: Cylindrical specimens (100 mm diameter × 200 mm height) were cast in accordance with SA TS 199:2023 [ 33 ] for the compressive strength test. GPC was placed in the moulds in two layers, each layer being tamped 25 times with a tamping rod (0.014 m 3 ). After each layer was tamped, the sides of the cylinder were further consolidated with 10 taps of a mallet to prevent the formation of voids. After 24 h, the specimens were demolded and covered with a plastic sheet for the required days of ambient curing. In total, 27 compression samples were tested through 3 trials of SCBA-based GPC preparation.

sections.heading: Test methods
paragraphs: Density was determined according to ASTM C138/C138M [ 34 ]. A compression test was performed according to ASTM C39/C39M [ 35 ]. The compressive strength was measured after the intended days of curing at the ambient temperature of the laboratory using Instron RD400 with 2000 kN capacity and 1 mm/min rate of displacement. At first, when the rubber capping was employed, the failure initiated in the top part of the specimens. Therefore, the capping was replaced with the timber for the later specimens. The specimens were mounted on the Instron RD400, and the crack patterns were observed during compressive loading.

sections.heading: Density
paragraphs: Densities were determined to verify whether the requirements for the concrete, as per SA TS 199:2023 [ 33 ], were satisfied. Overall densities of the SGPCs were lower than the CGPCs, in this study. The poor densification may reduce the compressive strength of SGPCs compared to CGPCs. A consistent reduction in density was observed between fresh and 7-day cured specimens, primarily due to moisture evaporation during the curing process. The measured density of CGPC-G was just outside the range of 2200–2600 kg/m 3  specified in SA TS 199:2023 [ 33 ] for geopolymer concrete for structural applications. This observed variation may be attributed to the geopolymerization gel structure created in the GPC. The modified GPC specimens (SGPC2.1-G, SGPC2.5-G, and SGPC3.1-G) consistently demonstrated lower densities compared to CGPC-G. This density reduction can be primarily attributed to the replacement of sodium silicate in the AA solution. But, SCBA-derived AA produces a comparatively weaker solution, which results in the formation of a less dense gel structure. Notably, SGPC2.5-G exhibited a marginal density increase compared to SGPC2.1-G due to the increment in SCBA content. However, SGPC3.1-G showed a subsequent density decrease, most likely resulting from lowered workability, which resulted in a less compacted specimen. The lowered workability may be attributed by the friction among the angular, irregular surface morphology of GGBS and the higher amorphous content that may enhance early strength gaining capacity of GGBS-based GPCs than the fly ash-based GPCs. These observations showed that SGPCs have lower densities than conventional GPC. The reduction observed for SGPCs with the incorporation of SCBA was due to the poor densification [ 36 ].

Fresh density, density at equilibrium and 28th day density of the specimens of Trial 2 are tabulated in Table  5 . The measured densities of CGPC-F and SGPC-F were within the expected range of 2200–2600 kg/m 3  specified in SA TS 199:2023 [ 33 ]. Similar to that in Trial 1, density reduced with time, primarily due to the moisture evaporation and densification. The density of the SGPC-Fs was reduced with the addition of SCBA content, may be due to the porous morphology of SCBA.

sections.heading: Compressive strength
paragraphs: Uniaxial compression tests resulted in distinct physical and mechanical behaviours across the different mixtures, attributed to variations in their polymerisation processes. These aspects are discussed below.

A visual inspection was carried out on specimens, with the specimen surface conditions shown in Fig.  8 . All specimens from Trial 1 and some of the specimens from Trials 2 and 3 that had relatively high SCBA contents were cracked before testing due to shrinkage. This observation corroborates the microcracking formation potential of GPCs, especially with higher GGBS content [ 37 ,  38 – 39 ]. The observation also suggests that high SCBA contents can result in high drying shrinkage cracking. However, no visible cracking was found prior to testing on the surface of the FA-based conventional mixture in Trial 2 and the counterpart mixture with the lowest SCBA content. Additionally, a brown colour change appeared on the surfaces of the SCBA-based AA incorporated GPC specimens. In Trial 3, surface pitting was detected on SGPC2.5-F. In addition, some surface damage was identified during the demoulding of SGPCS2.0-F and SGPCS1.5-F from the steel mould, even though canola oil had been applied to allow smooth demoulding. As discussed later, some of this demoulding-related damage may have caused a smaller strength to be achieved in Trial 3, which included superplasticisers. Fig. 8 Surface inspection before the compression test of various GPCs

The failure patterns under compression loading are shown in Fig.  9 . In Trial 1, for CGPC-G and SGPC2.1-G, cracks initiated at the top surface, with the reason being attributed to the use of a rubber capping. Therefore, timber capping was used for the rest of the testing, resulting in cracks being developed generally from the middle part of the cylinders. This damage was extended along vertical and inclined directions consistent with previous research [ 40 ,  41 ]and followed by spalling of the specimen’s surface, as also reported in Zhang et al. (2023) [ 42 ]. Exceptions were specimens SGPCS2.0-F and SGPCS1.5-F, in which the cracks initiated from the areas previously damaged in demoulding. Fig. 9 Failure patterns of various GPCs

The compressive strength test results are tabulated along with the coefficient of variance (CoV) and the number of samples in Table  6 . SGPC2.1-G, incorporating a limited amount of SCBA, achieved a compressive strength of 55% of the CGPC-G. This strength increased to 59% for SGPC2.5-G and further to 73% for SGPC3.1-G, indicating a positive influence of SCBA incorporation. These strength gains could be improved by incorporating a more intensive treatment of SCBA, which could enhance dissolution of silica in NaOH solution at a cost of more energy consumption. To this end, complex treatment processes reported in the related literature include continuous, rapid ball-milling [ 36 ], acid washing [ 13 ], and elevated temperatures while mixing with NaOH [ 7 ,  10 ]. In this research, simple magnetic stirring and ambient conditions were maintained, considering energy efficiency and user friendliness. Nonetheless, an increase in compressive strength was observed in mixtures with higher SCBA content, and this trend can be attributed to two potential factors: (1) Enhanced silica dissolution: The presence of SCBA may have facilitated the dissolution of silica to form sodium silicate to provide an alkaline environment, (2) Supplementary aluminosilicate source: Unreacted amorphous silica within the SCBA itself may have acted as an additional aluminosilicate source, contributing to the geopolymerization process.

An increase in CoV was observed with the incorporation of SCBA, this change being attributed to the reduced workability with time, which made the standard compaction operation ineffective. The CoV is very high for SGPC3.1-G because the workability was very low, and with time, it was further reduced.

In Trial 2, the strength gains of SGPC2.5-F, SGPC3.0-F, and SGPC3.5-F mixtures were, respectively, 13%, 9%, and 8% of that for CGPC-F, with COV being increased with a higher amount of SCBA incorporation. Primary factors that can improve these strength gains are a more intensive activation of the SCBA-derived AA and increasing the molarity of NaOH. As explained earlier, it was found that with increased SCBA, additional water was required to achieve workability. The added water decreased the concentration of the NaOH solution, leading to poor densification and compressive strength [ 36 ].

In Trial 3, even though the water requirement was reduced with the addition of superplasticiser, this change did not improve the compressive strength. It is acknowledged that two of the specimens were pre-damaged (SGPCS2.0-F and SGPCS1.5-F), but the strength of the one remaining specimen (SGPCS2.5-F) was still lower when compared to the counterpart from Trial 2 that lacked superplasticiser.

In summary, from experimental testing, the compressive strength of SCBA-based concrete ranged from 3.5 MPa to 5 MPa (excluding pre-damaged specimens). The SCBA-incorporated mixture that was based on GGBS-based GPC (Trial 1) was found to be promising as long as compressive strength was concerned as it achieved 73% of the strength of the conventional mixture. However, these mixtures also demonstrated relatively low workability and a high cracking tendency at the age of 7 days. Water or superplasticiser can be added to improve the workability, but it will affect the compressive strength gain. This aspect affects the placement of the mixture and may also adversely affect its durability. The fly ash-based mixtures that had SCBA contents (SGPCs) in Trial 2 did not achieve significant compressive strength when compared to the target CGPC-F (fc = 39.45 MPa), but they had the advantages of no/limited shrinkage cracking and acceptable workability. In Trial 3, due to only one specimen per mixture being available for compression testing, and observed physical damage during handling, the strength results from Trial 3 are considered preliminary. Hence, the results are presented only as an indicator for the potential of superplasticiser to increase the workability, not as a basis for strength comparison.

As discussed earlier, the introduction of SCBA in Trial 1 consistently increased CoV, with this trend being attributed to the low workability. The COV was reduced in Trial 2 with the addition of extra water to improve workability and hence compaction of SGPC-F. The results suggest that if acceptable workability is maintained to allow compaction, SCBA-based mixtures with acceptable CoV, e.g. less than 10% as demonstrated in Trial 2, can be made.

Based on the outcomes of all three trials, this study recommends advancing Trial 2 for further optimisation by exploring options of a) increasing the molarity of NaOH solution such that the additional water that was used to improve workability does not reduce the NaOH concentration below 6.5 M; b) partially replacing Na 2 SiO 3  with SCBA in different proportions with anticipation that this can improve compressive strength at a cost of the use of more virgin material (Na 2 SiO 3 ), and c) implementing a heat curing process which again will increase energy-consumption but is likely to add to the SCBA-based concrete strength.

Finally, as the study was focused on compressive strength, additional tests on other mechanical properties, such as tensile and bond strength, should be conducted to explore its potential for use in real-world applications. Considering the range of compressive strength, SGPC can potentially have non-structural applications, e.g. in manufacturing masonry units [ 43 ,  44 ].
The rationale behind employing a low-strength GPC over a CGPC was thus further investigated in the next section.

sections.heading: Environmental benefit analysis
paragraphs: A Life cycle assessment was conducted in accordance with AS ISO 14044, with global warming potential (GWP) selected as the environmental indicator for the analysis. The goal of environmental benefit analysis was to compare the overall environmental impact of CGPC and various SGPC.

A ‘cradle to gate’ approach was adopted for the carbon emission analysis, focusing on major emissions from raw material extraction until the end product leaves the gate of the production site [ 45 ]. The functional unit (FU) was defined as the CO 2 -equivalent emissions (kgCO 2 -e/kg) associated with the production of 1 m 3  of GPC [ 8 ]. This functional unit was consistently maintained across the whole study to enable a fair comparison between conventional and SCBA-based GPCs [ 46 ]. The CO 2 -equivalent (CO 2 -e) emissions were calculated by considering the contributions of CO 2 , CH 4 , NO 2  and synthetic gases evolved [ 8 ]. The analysis encompassed the stages such as raw material, production, collection, material preparation and GPC preparation. The system boundary is illustrated in Fig.  10 , outlining the activities and energy types involved in the production of GPC that contribute to emissions. Fig. 10 System boundary and processes of GPC production

The fly ash and factory-burnt SCB were directly procured from the manufacturer, Millmerran, and delivered to the production site. GGBS, sodium hydroxide, sodium silicate, and fine and coarse aggregates were obtained from a local distributor and transported to the laboratory, which served as the production site. The emissions during the production of raw materials were obtained from the literature and presented in the Table  7 . The CO 2  emissions associated with the production of SCBA were not considered in the analysis, as it is a waste product of a sugar milling factory, and then the bagasse was used for power production [ 47 ].

The analysis results are presented Table  9 . The study highlights how various factors influence carbon emissions, including the manufacturing of raw materials, transportation type, distance, processing methods, and mixture design. Among these, the proximity of manufacturers to the production site significantly affects the overall carbon footprint. SCBA-based AA-incorporated GPCs were found to have the least environmental impact. However, the reduction percentage decreased as SCBA content increased due to its treatment process. Incorporation of SCBA-based AA reduced embodied carbon by nearly 10% to 27% when transportation is included and about 11% to 30% when excluded.

The embodied carbon emissions associated with the treatment condition used in Trial 1 were higher than the treatment condition employed in Trials 2 and 3, highlighting the influence of the SCBA treatment method on the sustainability of SGPCs.

If we assume producing SCBA directly from SCB without prior burning, the efficient treatment conditions required to produce SCBA should be re-evaluated. Based on the TGA results of Adebisi et al. (2017), using a temperature of 500 °C results in approximately 77% mass loss for sugarcane bagasse. In contrast, for factory-burnt SCB, only about 25% mass loss occurs after furnace treatment. This significant difference means that a larger amount of SCB must be processed to obtain the required quantity of SCBA, which in turn would increase the number of furnace runs. These additional furnace runs would lead to higher energy consumption. Furthermore, the greater release of fumes from processing raw SCB could pose more serious environmental impacts compared to using pre-burnt SCBA obtained directly from sugar mills.

The findings indicate that the moderate (10%–30%) reduction in carbon footprint was accompanied by a dramatic decrease in compressive strength. While the low-strength concrete has potential to be explored for non-structural applications, future studies can focus on identifying a mixture design that can achieve a more optimal balance between sustainability and mechanical performance. Such mixtures would likely include partial replacement of Sodium Silicate with SCBA-based alkaline activator, or the use of other waste materials such as silica fume, or a more intensive treatment process as discussed in the Introduction section.

sections.heading: Concluding remarks
paragraphs: This study explored the development of a low-strength, environmentally friendly, and user-friendly GPC incorporating SCBA as a sustainable alternative for sodium silicate in the AA system. Factory-burnt SCB from Mackay Sugar, Queensland, was treated in a controlled temperature and duration to produce amorphous and low energy costing SCBA. Then the SCBA was mixed with NaOH solution to produce an alternative to the sodium silicate solution in GPC.

The key outcomes of the investigation can be summarised as follows: A simplified thermochemical method was developed for producing SCBA-based AA. The process involved furnace treatment of factory-burnt SCB at 700 °C for 90 min and 500 °C for 30 min, followed by mixing with a sodium hydroxide solution for 1 h at 400 rpm using a magnetic stirrer in a fume hood. Microstructural characterisation of factory-burnt SCB and SCBA (SEM, XRD, XRF, and TGA) showed that furnace treatment reduced particle size, removed unburnt SCBA particles, increased overall silica content, and improved thermal stability. Treating SCBA at 500 °C for 30 min proved more effective than factory-burnt SCB and SCBA treated at 700 °C for 90 min in terms of both amorphous silica content and embodied carbon. Density results showed that GPC produced with conventional alkaline activators had higher density, while those made with SCBA-based activators exhibited lower density. The resulting SCBA-based AA incorporated GPCs exhibited a compressive strength in the range of 3 MPa to 5 MPa across three trials, excluding damaged specimens. The tests indicated that CoV of compressive strength can increase with the addition of SCBA, with this trend being attributable to decreased workability. If workability is achieved consistently (as in Trial 2), CoV can be reduced to acceptable values (less than 10%). Fly ash-based mixtures demonstrated less susceptibility than GGBS-based mixtures to surface cracking throughout the ambient curing period. Life cycle-based embodied carbon analysis indicated that the use of SCBA-based AA in GPC can reduce the carbon footprint by 10% to 27% when the location is involved and by 11% to 30% when the location is not involved. SGPC1-F exhibited the lowest embodied carbon. These reductions evidenced the potential contribution of low-strength SCBA-based AA-incorporated GPC for non-structural applications.

In summary, the study recommends advancing Trial 2 by optimising the AA through increasing the molarity of NaOH and partially substituting SCBA in different proportions to improve compressive strength while considering the trade-off of increased virgin material utilisation. Furthermore, implementing a heat-curing process is proposed to enhance mechanical performance, acknowledging the associated increase in energy consumption. As this investigation focused primarily on compressive strength, further testing of other mechanical properties, such as tensile and bond strength, is proposed to evaluate the feasibility of SCBA-based GPC for practical applications.

The study demonstrated the viability of SCBA as a potential alternative to commercial sodium silicate in the AA system for producing low-strength concrete with reduced environmental impact. This approach aligns with circular economy goals and adds value to agricultural waste as a sustainable construction material. Although the resulting SGPC cannot be used in structural applications, it may be suitable for non-structural applications with the benefit of lower embodied carbon.
